claims.uncertainty: Skeletal muscle is used as one clear boundary case. The lesson does not attempt to catalogue every postmitotic or multinucleate cell type.

claims.statement: A stem cell is defined by its capacity for self-renewal and production of differentiated progeny, not by continuous division; some stem-cell populations can be quiescent until activated, while active stem cells at the crypt base supply differentiating daughters to the colonic lining.
claims.scope: The general definition of a stem cell and the narrower active crypt-base example used in this lesson.
claims.uncertainty: Stem-cell cycling patterns differ between tissues and physiological states. The lesson contrasts quiescent satellite cells with active crypt-base populations only to separate defining capacity from continuous activity; it does not catalogue stem-cell states.

claims.statement: In current scientific usage, a theory is a concise, coherent and predictive explanation for a broad range of phenomena that can integrate many hypotheses; hypotheses may be narrower explanations, the terminology varies between disciplines, and scientific knowledge remains open to revision when evidence warrants it.
claims.scope: The distinction among scientific theory, hypothesis and everyday guess used in this lesson, without treating the terms as a universal promotion ladder.
claims.uncertainty: Scientific fields do not use theory and hypothesis with perfect consistency. The lesson therefore describes their typical differences in breadth and explanatory role and makes evidence, scope and revisability more important than the label.

claims.statement: Rudolf Virchow's Cellularpathologie, first published in 1858, established the concept that diseases can be diagnosed by analysing the cells in a patient's tissue, which is the basis of histological diagnosis today.
claims.scope: The historical origin of histological diagnosis as a general medical practice, used to show what cell theory licensed in medicine.
claims.uncertainty: This is a statement about the origin and general basis of a discipline. It carries no diagnostic criterion, no test performance, and nothing about how any particular specimen should be interpreted, and the lesson makes no such claim.

claims.statement: A crypt in the human descending colon holds approximately 700 cells, arranged about 32 along its length and about 22 around its circumference.
claims.scope: The cell population and cell-wise dimensions of a single crypt in the descending colon, used for simplified renewal arithmetic, a base-to-surface migration estimate and a projected opening-width estimate.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is for the descending colon and comes from a modelling study that assembled it from reported measurements; crypt size varies along the colon, between people, and with disease. The lesson distinguishes crypt depth from projected surface width and labels both geometric calculations as estimates rather than measurements from the source.

claims.statement: Within the lesson's simplified circular model, 22 cells of about 10 micrometres around a crypt perimeter imply a circumference near 220 micrometres and an opening diameter near 70 micrometres.
claims.scope: A projected crypt-opening width used only for one-dimensional comparisons with stipulated surface-view resolution thresholds.
claims.uncertainty: This is a geometric inference from model parameters, not a morphometric measurement. It assumes circular geometry and 10 micrometre cells, does not include lumen-wall thickness, and supplies no opening-to-opening separation or surface density. Crypt depth is a different, perpendicular dimension and is not used for surface visibility.

claims.statement: A colonic crypt is an invagination of the epithelial lining whose base is the stem-cell niche; cells differentiate as they migrate upward and are fully differentiated at the crypt top, Wnt signalling decreases progressively up the crypt axis, colonocytes maintain the integrity of the epithelial barrier, and mucins secreted by goblet cells form the mucus layer that protects against pathogen invasion.
claims.scope: The layout of the colonic crypt, the direction of migration and differentiation, the decline of Wnt signalling along the crypt axis, and the barrier and mucus functions of the epithelium, at the level of detail a first lesson needs.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson omits the specific molecular signal and treats the gradient qualitatively; the mechanism by which a cell reads its position is the subject of a later lesson in this block and is not established here. The account describes the healthy adult human colon and is not a description of disease.

claims.statement: Continuous intestinal epithelial barrier function requires a contiguous cell layer and the junctions that seal the paracellular space, while epithelial cells also support transcellular transport through individual cells; continuous tissue-level exclusion, paracellular permeability and transcellular permeability are therefore related but distinct properties.
claims.scope: The distinction needed to classify continuous barrier coverage as an emergent tissue property without denying permeability and transport properties of individual epithelial cells.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson uses only the high-level distinction among transcellular, paracellular and continuous tissue-level properties. It does not teach molecular permeability pathways, disease mechanisms, measurement, or treatment.

claims.statement: In the bounded tissue-level sense used in this lesson, spatially or temporally coordinated behaviours of interacting cells can produce population properties absent from an isolated cell; continuous epithelial barrier coverage, a positional signalling gradient and coordinated tissue renewal are examples tied to organisation rather than cell number alone.
claims.scope: An operational use of emergence for the three epithelial examples taught and assessed in this lesson.
claims.uncertainty: Emergence has multiple technical senses across biology, systems science and philosophy. The lesson's two-part disruption test is a practical classifier for these examples, not a necessary-and-sufficient definition for every emergent phenomenon; each example retains its separate empirical source and boundary.

claims.statement: Much of the colonic epithelium renews on a three-to-five-day timescale, with absorptive enterocytes replaced every four to five days; a second, independent report gives the same three-to-five-day population-level interval for the human intestinal epithelium.
claims.scope: The bulk turnover interval of the healthy adult human colonic epithelium, used for a simplified steady-state production estimate and to motivate coordinated renewal.
claims.uncertainty: Reported intervals differ between studies, between regions of the intestine, and between the cell types within one crypt; the same review notes that some enteroendocrine cells persist far longer than enterocytes, and self-renewing lineages persist. The lesson therefore does not claim that every crypt cell is replaced on one schedule.

claims.statement: Cells in the lower half of the human colonic crypt migrate upward at an average speed of around 4 micrometres per hour.
claims.scope: The measured average upward migration speed in the lower half of a normal human colonic crypt, used as an independent consistency check on the renewal interval.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is reported for the lower half of the crypt only. Extending it over the whole climb to estimate a base-to-surface transit time assumes a speed that does not change with height, which the source does not report and which may be false. The lesson states that assumption where it makes the estimate.

claims.statement: Quantitative research on the normal and the neoplastic human colon is conducted at the level of the crypt and its cell populations, rather than by cataloguing single cells in isolation.
claims.scope: The level of biological organisation at which published colon research operates, used to connect the lesson's emergence argument to how the tissue is actually studied.
claims.uncertainty: This is an observation about two published works and the practice they represent, not a survey of the field, and it says nothing about routine diagnostic practice, criteria, or reporting. Single-cell methods are also used in colon research, and their existence does not conflict with the point being made about crypt-level organisation.

claims.statement: An adult human body holds cells of order 10 to the 13: about 3.0 x 10^13 by one estimate for a 70 kg reference man, and about 36 trillion for an adult male and 28 trillion for an adult female by a later independent estimate. The colon carries about 3.8 x 10^13 bacteria, which is the same order of magnitude as the body's own cell count.
claims.scope: Order-of-magnitude counts of human cells in a reference adult body and of bacteria in the colon, used to show what the epithelial sheet stands between.
claims.uncertainty: The two estimates disagree by tens of per cent and agree on the order of magnitude, which is the only part the lesson uses. Both are constructions for a reference body rather than measurements of any person, both depend on assumptions about which cell types dominate the count, and the bacterial figure is derived from a density per gram of stool and an assumed colon volume.

terms.definition: The basic bounded unit of living tissue that is itself alive and maintains an organised internal state. Cells continue cellular lineages from pre-existing cells, but an individual living cell need not be able to divide: mature skeletal muscle fibres are living cells that do not divide. The everyday senses of the word, a room in a prison, a box in a spreadsheet, or a source of current in a battery, carry none of this biology.

The established framework that cells are the basic living units of plant and animal tissues and that cells within ongoing lineages continue pre-existing cellular lineages rather than appearing from non-cellular material. Tissues may also contain abundant cell-derived extracellular material. Division is the usual lineage-preserving route, but specialised cells can form by other processes such as fusion of pre-existing myoblasts into a skeletal muscle fibre. The lineage principle does not address the origin of the first cells. Established in Berlin in 1838 and 1839 and refined afterwards, cell theory fixed the unit of biological organisation while remaining revisable within its scope.

In current scientific usage, a broad, coherent and predictive explanatory framework that integrates observations and hypotheses and remains revisable as evidence changes. A hypothesis is a more specific proposition that evidence can evaluate and that may test, extend or apply a theory; the terms are not consecutive rungs in a universal promotion ladder, and usage varies between fields. The everyday sense of a private guess is different and is the sense this lesson sets aside.

alignment.note: No earlier lesson holds a glossary entry for this word, so nothing is being overridden. This lesson adopts PREM-SCI-010's attention to scope, assumptions and evidentiary tests, while making explicit that theory and hypothesis differ in explanatory role and breadth rather than forming a universal promotion ladder. The learner's everyday sense of a guess is named and separated from the scientific usage in prose.

terms.definition: A power-of-ten description of a quantity's approximate scale. Two quantities are of the same order when their ratio is nearer to 1 than to 10. This lesson compares sizes and counts by order of magnitude first and only then looks at the digits, because every quantity it uses is an estimate for a reference body or a representative case.

alignment.note: Adopts the meaning PREM-QNT-005 already gives the term, a power-of-ten description of a quantity's approximate scale, and does not restate the arithmetic. This lesson is where that arithmetic earns its keep: every size, threshold, and count in cell biology is a band rather than a constant, and comparing bands by their power of ten is how the block reasons throughout.

terms.definition: The smallest separation at which an instrument or eye distinguishes two spatial features as separate, or the finest spatial detail it resolves. Resolution does not by itself determine detection or localisation: a labelled or high-contrast feature narrower than the resolution limit may still produce a detectable signal, while its width, shape, or nearby neighbours remain unresolved. Resolution belongs to the imaging system and conditions, not to the specimen alone.

The factor by which an instrument enlarges the apparent size of an object. Magnification and spatial resolution are separate quantities: enlarging an image past an instrument's resolution limit produces a larger blur without revealing finer spatial detail. Magnification alone also does not determine detection or localisation, which depend on contrast, labelling, sampling and noise.

A millionth of a metre, and a thousandth of a millimetre, written µm. It is the working unit of cell biology: cells are measured in tens of micrometres and tissue structures in hundreds. Spatial detail finer than about a quarter of a micrometre is not resolved by a conventional light microscope, although a sufficiently contrasting or labelled sub-resolution feature may still be detected or localised.

Organised biological material made from one or more cell types and the extracellular material associated with them. The mix of cell types, the amount and form of extracellular material, and whether the cells are directly attached vary between tissues. A tissue function may depend on organisation, but it need not be absent from every component cell.

A sheet of cells covering a surface or lining a cavity, joined to its neighbours so that the sheet is continuous. The colonic epithelium is one cell thick and separates the contents of the gut from the tissue beneath it.

The open space inside a tube or hollow organ, and the side of an epithelium that faces it. In the colon the lumen holds the gut contents, including the bacterial population the epithelium keeps out of the tissue.

Movement or permeability through an epithelial cell, across its membranes and interior. It is a property to which an individual cell contributes directly and is distinct from continuous barrier coverage across a tissue.

Movement or permeability through the space between neighbouring epithelial cells, regulated by the junctions that join those cells. It depends on cell-to-cell organisation and differs from a transcellular route through one cell.

A blind-ended tube of epithelium sunk into the wall of the large intestine, holding roughly 700 cells in the descending colon. Dividing cells sit at its base, their daughters move upward and take on specialised jobs as they go, and worn cells are shed from the surface into the lumen. It is the structure this whole module follows.

A cell with the capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny. The definition is about capacity rather than continuous activity: some stem-cell populations are quiescent until activated, while others cycle actively. In this lesson the term names the active stem cells at the crypt base that supply the differentiating cells of the lining. Lessons 08 and 10 of this block develop what division involves and what happens when its control fails.

In this lesson's bounded tissue-level sense, a property produced by the spatial or temporal organisation of interacting cells that is not a property of one isolated cell. For the epithelial examples here, test whether the stated property is absent from one cell and is lost when the relevant arrangement is disrupted. Continuous epithelial exclusion across an area is emergent in this sense; one cell's boundary and transcellular permeability are not. Other fields use emergence in additional technical senses, so this operational test is not a universal definition.

Which components sit where, what each is joined to, and what each is doing. Organisation is what an emergent property belongs to, and it is the variable that matters: the same components in the same number, unarranged, show none of the properties the arranged population shows.

Terminology continuity

The course terminology ledger was read before the glossary was designed. Fourteen of the sixteen entries introduce terms no published lesson currently owns: cell, cell theory, resolution, magnification, micrometre, tissue, epithelium, lumen, transcellular permeability, paracellular permeability, colonic crypt, stem cell, emergent property, and biological organisation. Two declare an alignment block in glossary.json.

  • order of magnitude — adopt from PREM-QNT-005, which owns the powers-and-orders-of-magnitude sense. The meaning is unchanged and the arithmetic is not re-taught. This lesson is where that arithmetic does its work, because every size, threshold, and count in cell biology is a band rather than a constant.
  • theory — adopt from PREM-SCI-010. No prior published lesson holds a glossary entry for this word, so the block brief's ruling is recorded here as an adoption rather than as the resolution of a ledger collision. The fourth scene keeps the earlier lesson's attention to scope, assumptions and evidentiary tests, adds the evidence-supported distinction between a broad theory and a more specific hypothesis, and explicitly rejects a universal promotion ladder. It also separates scientific usage from the learner's everyday sense of a guess.

Source use and rights

Eighteen sources support the factual claims. Every one was used for facts only, followed by an independent instructional structure and original expression; no source is quoted, adapted, redrawn, or reorganised anywhere in the pack, and no example, question, table, figure, or dataset is taken from any of them. Complete locators, use records, rights evidence, and dated agent-access checks appear in references.json.

  • source-ashraf-eye-resolution, Ashraf, Chapiro and Mantiuk, Resolution limit of the eye: the 1 minute of arc standard behind 20/20 vision, its equivalence to 60 pixels per degree, and the measured foveal limit near 94 pixels per degree. Converting that angle to a length at a stated viewing distance is this pack's own arithmetic and is presented as such.
  • source-li-cell-size, Li, Rycaj, Chen and Tang: that the majority of animal cells are 10 to 20 µm in diameter.
  • source-hatton-cell-count, Hatton and colleagues, The human cell count and size distribution: total body cell counts of about 36 trillion for an adult male and 28 trillion for an adult female, and the spread of human cell sizes over about seven orders of magnitude.
  • source-sender-cell-numbers, Sender, Fuchs and Milo: 3.0 × 10^13 human cells and 3.8 × 10^13 bacteria for a 70 kg reference man, and 3.8 × 10^13 bacteria in the colon.
  • source-vanderwath-crypt-model, van der Wath and colleagues: about 700 cells in a descending-colon crypt arranged 32 along the length and 22 around the perimeter, a mean cell radius of 5 µm, and replacement of the human intestinal epithelium every 3 to 5 days.
  • source-nguyen-colonic-crypt, Nguyen, Lausten and Boman: the crypt base as the stem-cell niche, differentiation during upward migration, Wnt signalling decreasing up the crypt axis, renewal every 3 to 5 days with enterocytes replaced every 4 to 5, and the barrier and mucus roles of the epithelium.
  • source-baker-crypt-dynamics, Baker and colleagues: the measured average migration speed of about 4 µm per hour in the lower half of the human colonic crypt, and evidence that quantitative colon research operates at crypt level.
  • source-galbraith-resolution-limit, Galbraith and Galbraith: the roughly 250 nm lateral resolution limit of conventional light microscopy, and that enlarging past that limit separates nothing further.
  • source-seeman-dna, Seeman: the DNA double helix at about 20 angstroms, that is 2 nm, across.
  • source-kutschera-leeuwenhoek, Kutschera: publication of Hooke's Micrographia in 1665 and Hooke's definition there of the term cell.
  • source-peters-hooke, Peters: Hooke's cork observations, his comparison of cork with a mushroom rather than with plant tissue, and his separate note that cells in plants were filled with fluid. This article exists to correct the popular retelling of the episode, and it is cited here to avoid repeating the version it corrects.
  • source-kettenmann-virchow, Kettenmann: cell theory established in Berlin in 1838 and 1839 by Schleiden for plants and Schwann for animals, Virchow's Cellularpathologie of 1858, and the origin of histological diagnosis.
  • source-mullerwille-cell-theory, Müller-Wille: the standard three-part statement of the tenets, including that cells arise from division of pre-existing cells, and the point that the propositions were refined over decades.
  • source-alberts-muscle-fusion, Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell: the boundary case that a multinucleate skeletal muscle fibre forms by fusion of pre-existing myoblasts and does not arise directly through one cell division, and the distinction between a stem cell's capacity for self-renewal and differentiation and whether that population is actively cycling or quiescent.
  • source-alberts-extracellular-matrix, Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell: that animal tissues include extracellular material whose amount and organisation vary greatly between tissue types, so a joined population of one cell kind is not a general definition of tissue.
  • source-weisberg-how-science-works, Weisberg and Thanukos, How Science Works: the distinction between broad theories and potentially narrower hypotheses, the variability of those labels between fields, and the revisability of scientific knowledge.
  • source-odenwald-epithelial-barrier, Odenwald and Turner: continuous epithelial barrier function requiring a contiguous layer and sealed paracellular space while individual cells support transcellular transport.
  • source-dossantos-tissue-self-organization, dos Santos and Liberali: that tissue patterns, positional information and renewal depend on spatially and temporally coordinated cell populations and are described as emergent at tissue level.

Three of these sources carry NonCommercial or NoDerivatives terms, and several others retain publisher copyright or appear as publisher-terms manuscripts. Boundaries and exceptions

Every learner task has a text-first path. The scale-ladder diagram and the cork micrograph both carry long descriptions that state the relationships and the conclusion drawn from them, so no task in the lesson depends on seeing either figure. All tables are original semantic text.

The clinical material is illustrative. The patient having a colonoscopy in the seventh scene, the imaging system's stipulated 0.1 mm of delivered detail, the invented research team in the assessment and its 40 µm instrument, and the hand lens in the practice scene are all constructions for teaching. No source in this pack reports the resolution of any real clinical instrument, and the lesson states that plainly where the figures are used. The wrap-up carries an explicit teaching-example boundary, describes no real patient, service, device, or procedure, and contains no diagnostic criterion, threshold, test performance, or statement of what any finding would mean. Nothing in the pack is medical advice.

Correction to the 0.1.0 finalization

The academic review of this candidate raised, as a major finding, that diagrams/scale-ladder.diagram.json declared a largest-to-smallest ladder while placing the 100 µm unaided-eye threshold above a crypt of 320 to 640 µm, with its own edge label stating that the crypt is the larger of the two. The finalization recorded that finding as incorporated and listed "Reordered the scale ladder" among its material changes.

The scene prose was corrected. The diagram file was not opened, so the rendered rung order and the relationship list still contradicted the caption above them. The adjudication artifact is left as written, because it is the record of what was decided and reporting it accurately matters more than making it look right in hindsight.

This correction applies the repair the finalization already recorded: the crypt now sits at the top of the ladder and each threshold sits between the two structures it separates, which is also the point the scene was making at that time.

The academic review of the 0.1.1 candidate then identified a different dimensional error: crypt base-to-surface length cannot establish what a surface view resolves. This finalization therefore replaces that visibility comparison with a labelled geometric inference for projected opening width and removes every inference about opening spacing or density that the available data do not support. The current adjudication records that post-review change against the frozen 0.1.1 candidate.
